content: Broccoli is a member of the Brassicaceae family, previously known as Cruciferae, and is classified under the Italica Cultivar Group of the species Brassica oleracea. It is characterized by its dense clusters of fleshy, green flower heads, which are arranged in a tree-like structure on branches that grow from a thick, edible stalk. These flower heads are surrounded by leaves. Broccoli is closely related to cauliflower, another cultivar of the same species, but differs in color, with broccoli being green and cauliflower typically white. In the United States, the term broccoli generally refers to the variety with a single large head, which is sometimes called Calabrese in the United Kingdom. In the UK, other forms of broccoli, such as sprouting types with underdeveloped flower buds, are also sold under the same name. The term broccoli is derived from the Latin word broccolo, which is a diminutive form meaning sprout. Broccoli is a cultivated variety of wild cabbage (Brassica oleracea), which originated along the northern and western Mediterranean coasts. This wild cabbage was domesticated thousands of years ago and subsequently bred into various forms, including broccoli, cauliflower, cabbage, kale, kohlrabi, and Brussels sprouts, all of which belong to the same species. Historical references to broccoli are somewhat ambiguous, but the Roman naturalist Pliny the Elder described a vegetable resembling broccoli, suggesting that it was cultivated in ancient Rome for culinary purposes. Some scholars also identify broccoli in the Roman cookbook attributed to Apicius. Broccoli was primarily an Italian vegetable for centuries, as its name implies, and was initially a sprouting variety rather than the single large-headed type commonly seen today. Broccoli was first mentioned in France in 1560, but it remained relatively unknown in England until the 18th century. In 1724, Philip Miller's Gardener's Dictionary described broccoli as a stranger in England, referring to it as sprout colli-flower or Italian asparagus. In the American colonies, Thomas Jefferson, an avid gardener, planted broccoli at Monticello in 1767 alongside other vegetables such as radishes, lettuce, and cauliflower. However, broccoli remained an exotic vegetable in American gardens. In 1775, John Randolph described broccoli in his gardening treatise, noting that its stems could be eaten like asparagus and its heads like cauliflower. Italian immigrants introduced broccoli to North America by 1806, but it did not gain widespread popularity until the 1920s. Commercial cultivation in the United States began with the D'Arrigo brothers, Italian immigrants who started planting broccoli in San Jose, California, in 1922. Their brand, Andy Boy, named after Stephano D'Arrigo's young son, Andrew, helped popularize broccoli through radio advertisements. There are three main types of broccoli commonly grown. The most familiar variety, often called Calabrese in the UK and simply broccoli in North America, has large green heads measuring 10–20 cm and thick stalks. It is named after Calabria, Italy, where it was first cultivated, and is a cool-season annual crop. Sprouting broccoli produces multiple smaller heads with thin stalks and is typically planted in May for harvest during the winter or early the following year in temperate climates. Romanesco broccoli is notable for its unique fractal-like appearance and yellow-green color. It belongs to the Botrytis (cauliflower) cultivar group. Another variety, purple cauliflower, is a type of broccoli sold in southern Italy, Spain, and the UK. It has a cauliflower-like head composed of tiny flower buds, sometimes with a purple tint at the tips. Broccoli thrives in cool weather and does not perform well in hot summer conditions. Other cultivar groups of Brassica oleracea include cabbage (Capitata Group), cauliflower (Botrytis Group), kale and collard greens (Acephala Group), kohlrabi (Gongylodes Group), and Brussels sprouts (Gemmifera Group). Chinese broccoli (Alboglabra Group) is another cultivar of the same species. Broccoli is typically boiled or steamed but can also be eaten raw, and it has become a popular addition to hors d'oeuvre trays. Nutritionally, broccoli is rich in vitamin C and soluble fiber. It contains several bioactive compounds with anti-cancer properties, including diindolylmethane and selenium. The compound 3,3'-Diindolylmethane found in broccoli has demonstrated potent anti-viral, anti-bacterial, and anti-cancer effects by modulating the innate immune response. Broccoli also contains glucoraphanin, which can be converted into sulforaphane, a compound with anti-cancer properties. However, boiling broccoli can reduce its health benefits. High consumption of broccoli has been associated with a reduced risk of aggressive prostate cancer. Additionally, broccoli leaves are edible and contain significantly more beta-carotene than the florets. In popular culture, broccoli gained attention in 1928 when it was still relatively novel in the United States. A cartoon in The New Yorker depicted a mother and child at the dinner table, with the mother saying, It's broccoli, dear, and the child responding, I say it's spinach, and I say the hell with it. In politics, U.S. President George H.W. Bush famously expressed his dislike for broccoli during his presidency, prompting the broccoli agriculture lobby to send several tons of the vegetable to the White House. The broccoli was subsequently donated to the Capital Area Food Bank. His son, President George W. Bush, later remarked in 2004 that he did not mind broccoli but preferred the florets over the stalks.
